sn12.1:1.1: For an overview of this topic, see my Introduction to the Saṁyutta Nikāya.
sn12.1:1.3: In a shift from the previous book, there is no interaction or dialogue; the teaching is a direct address by the Buddha.
sn12.1:2.2: “Knowledge” (_veda_) was that of the immortal gods, so knowledge itself is immortal, while ignorance, being perishable, traps the fool in suffering for life after life. Knowledge and ignorance are part of the mortal condition (Atharva Veda 11.8.23). “A man crosses death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge” (Īśa Upaniṣad 11; cf. Paiṅgala Upaniṣad 2.11, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
sn12.1:2.3: A person becomes something good by good deeds, bad by bad deeds (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
sn12.1:2.4: One who is dying becomes mere consciousness, driven by previous knowledge and actions (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
sn12.1:2.5: A virtuous man abandons his old form and fashions a new, better one as a god, etc. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.4).
sn12.1:2.14: There is no corresponding “dependent cessation”. The ending of dependent origination is Nibbana, extinguishment.
